questions.question: State the interaction between magnetic poles.
questions.modelAnswer: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.
markingPoints: Like poles repel
unlike poles attract.

questions.question: Distinguish permanent magnets from induced magnets.
questions.modelAnswer: A permanent magnet produces its own field and remains magnetised. An induced magnet becomes magnetic in another field, is attracted to the inducing magnet and usually loses magnetism when removed.
markingPoints: A permanent magnet produces its own field and remains magnetised. An induced magnet becomes magnetic in another field, is attracted to the inducing magnet and usually loses magnetism when removed.

questions.question: Define a magnetic field and state its direction around a bar magnet.
questions.modelAnswer: A region where a magnet or magnetic material experiences a force; direction is from north to south outside the magnet.
markingPoints: A region where a magnet or magnetic material experiences a force
direction is from north to south outside the magnet.

questions.question: Explain why a compass points approximately north.
questions.modelAnswer: Its needle is a small magnet; Earth has a magnetic field; the needle aligns with the field, so its north-seeking pole points towards magnetic north.
markingPoints: Its needle is a small magnet
Earth has a magnetic field
the needle aligns with the field, so its north-seeking pole points towards magnetic north.

questions.question: Describe the magnetic field around a straight current-carrying wire.
questions.modelAnswer: Concentric circles centred on the wire; direction is given by the right-hand grip rule; field strength increases with current and decreases with distance.
markingPoints: Concentric circles centred on the wire
direction is given by the right-hand grip rule
field strength increases with current and decreases with distance.

questions.question: Explain how to increase the strength of an electromagnet made from a solenoid.
questions.modelAnswer: Increase current; increase turns per unit length; add a soft-iron core; these increase/concentrate the magnetic field.
markingPoints: Increase current
increase turns per unit length
add a soft-iron core
these increase/concentrate the magnetic field.

questions.question: Explain the motor effect.
questions.modelAnswer: A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force; the conductor’s field interacts with the external field; force direction is perpendicular to current and field and is found using Fleming’s left-hand rule.
markingPoints: A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force
the conductor’s field interacts with the external field
force direction is perpendicular to current and field and is found using Fleming’s left-hand rule.

questions.question: Explain how a simple d.c. motor keeps rotating.
questions.modelAnswer: Opposite sides of the coil carry currents in opposite directions and experience opposite forces, producing a turning effect. The split-ring commutator reverses current every half-turn, keeping the turning effect in the same rotational direction.
markingPoints: Opposite sides of the coil carry currents in opposite directions and experience opposite forces, producing a turning effect. The split-ring commutator reverses current every half-turn, keeping the turning effect in the same rotational direction.

questions.question: State the conditions needed to induce a potential difference.
questions.modelAnswer: A conductor must cut magnetic field lines, or the magnetic field through a conductor/coil must change; faster change gives a larger induced p.d.
markingPoints: A conductor must cut magnetic field lines, or the magnetic field through a conductor/coil must change
faster change gives a larger induced p.d.

questions.question: Explain how the direction of induced current is determined.
questions.modelAnswer: The induced current creates a magnetic field that opposes the change that produced it; this is Lenz’s law and is consistent with energy conservation.
markingPoints: The induced current creates a magnetic field that opposes the change that produced it
this is Lenz’s law and is consistent with energy conservation.

questions.question: Explain how a moving-coil microphone converts sound into an electrical signal.
questions.modelAnswer: Sound vibrates a diaphragm attached to a coil; the coil moves in a magnetic field; changing flux induces an alternating p.d.; its variation represents the sound wave.
markingPoints: Sound vibrates a diaphragm attached to a coil
the coil moves in a magnetic field
changing flux induces an alternating p.d.
its variation represents the sound wave.

questions.question: Explain how a loudspeaker produces sound.
questions.modelAnswer: Alternating current in a coil within a magnetic field produces a changing force; the coil and cone vibrate; they create pressure variations in air, producing sound.
markingPoints: Alternating current in a coil within a magnetic field produces a changing force
the coil and cone vibrate
they create pressure variations in air, producing sound.

questions.question: Explain how a transformer works and why it requires alternating current.
questions.modelAnswer: AC in the primary creates a changing magnetic field in the iron core; changing flux links the secondary; an alternating p.d. is induced. DC would not continuously change flux, so no continuous secondary p.d. is induced.
markingPoints: AC in the primary creates a changing magnetic field in the iron core
changing flux links the secondary
an alternating p.d. is induced. DC would not continuously change flux, so no continuous secondary p.d. is induced.

questions.question: Distinguish step-up and step-down transformers using turn numbers.
questions.modelAnswer: Step-up: more turns on secondary than primary, so secondary p.d. is higher. Step-down: fewer secondary turns, so secondary p.d. is lower.
markingPoints: Step-up: more turns on secondary than primary, so secondary p.d. is higher. Step-down: fewer secondary turns, so secondary p.d. is lower.

questions.question: A transformer has 1200 primary turns and 80 secondary turns. The primary p.d. is 230 V. Calculate the secondary p.d.
questions.modelAnswer:
Vₚ ÷ Vₛ = Nₚ ÷ Nₛ
Vₛ = VₚNₛ ÷ Nₚ
Vₛ = 230 × 80 ÷ 1200
Vₛ = 15.3 V
markingPoints: Vₚ ÷ Vₛ = Nₚ ÷ Nₛ
Vₛ = VₚNₛ ÷ Nₚ

questions.question: An ideal transformer supplies 12 V at 3.0 A. The primary potential difference is 230 V. Calculate the primary current.
questions.modelAnswer:
VₚIₚ = VₛIₛ
Iₚ = VₛIₛ ÷ Vₚ
Iₚ = 12 × 3.0 ÷ 230
Iₚ = 0.157 A ≈ 0.16 A
markingPoints: VₚIₚ = VₛIₛ
Iₚ = VₛIₛ ÷ Vₚ

questions.question: Describe how to map the magnetic field around a bar magnet.
questions.modelAnswer: Place paper over the magnet. Put a plotting compass at many positions and mark the needle direction. Move the compass so its tail begins at the previous head and repeat. Join marks into smooth field lines with arrows from north to south.
markingPoints: Place paper over the magnet. Put a plotting compass at many positions and mark the needle direction. Move the compass so its tail begins at the previous head and repeat. Join marks into smooth field lines with arrows from north to south.

questions.question: A transformer changes 230 V to 12 V. The primary has 1150 turns. Calculate secondary turns.
questions.modelAnswer:
Vₚ ÷ Vₛ = Nₚ ÷ Nₛ
Nₛ = NₚVₛ ÷ Vₚ
Nₛ = 1150 × 12 ÷ 230
Nₛ = 60 turns
markingPoints: Vₚ ÷ Vₛ = Nₚ ÷ Nₛ
Nₛ = NₚVₛ ÷ Vₚ
Nₛ = 60 turns
